Question: Are improvised explosive devices used in the military?
Answer: Improvised Explosive Devices (IEDs) are the weapon of choice for guerrilla armies and special operations forces. Modifying an artillery shell, for example, and turning it into a booby trap does not only require special skills but it’s also not free of risks. Therefore, conventional armies hesitate to train their soldiers in the art of IED manufacturing. In addition, some Western armies consider that the use of IEDs violates international conventions. However, despite these hesitations, desperate times sometimes require desperate measures. A workshop near the frontline where improvised bombs, grenades, and mines are manufactured. I visited this location and support the soldiers that are working there with equipment. (Picture taken by one of my friends) In Ukraine, many regular units now manufacture their own booby traps. On the zero line (the line closest to the enemy) you can find hundreds of different kinds of IEDs that are not only used against enemy infantry and tanks but also against drones. At the same time, Ukrainian soldiers learn how to neutralize the explosive traps the enemy has set up. One of my friends from Germany is running such a IEDD (IED disposal) training course. A soldier in Ukraine is working on a IED during a training course. (Picture: X-Intelligence GmbH, with friendly permission) The current lack of ammunition on the Ukrainian side has accelerated these developments. While in earlier stages of the war, abandoned enemy ammunition depots had been more or less ignored by frontline troops, they now bring the ordnance to workshops near the frontline where the ammunition gets “recycled”: The primers, for example, are removed and used to make detonators (for FPV drones) while the explosive (usually TNT) is carefully melted and reused in a variety of explosive devices. These improvised workshops play an important role in Ukraine’s defense efforts. They help to compensate for the lack of ammunition supplies from the West. Question: Is anyone keeping count of the thousands of NATO mercenaries killed in Ukraine?
Answer: I follow some of the pro-Russian online channels that publish information regarding the fate of foreign volunteer fighters in Ukraine. These Russian bloggers are certainly the biggest liars under the sun but when it comes to foreigners in Ukraine who were killed in action, their numbers are usually quite accurate. Stefan Zander, a former German Army soldier, was killed last week on the Ukrainian frontline. (Picture: Ukrainian Pravda) Sometimes, they even correct themselves when a foreigner they had declared dead before suddenly turns up alive and kicking on the frontline. If I remember correctly, there were around ten foreign fighters killed in action (KIA) during the last 30 days. Most of them were from the so-called “Norman brigade”. This is a bit unusual as the monthly KIA numbers are usually a bit lower. Altogether, there are maybe a few hundred foreigners who lost their lives for the freedom of Ukraine, certainly not “thousands”. All of them are heroes. Question: After Bradley infantry vehicle dominated a T90 tank, can we say that infantry undisputedly won the infantry vs tankers debate?
Answer: The video of a Bradley shooting up a T-90 shows excellent situational awareness, training, and coordination on the part of the Ukrainian Bradley crew. At the same time, it shows that these qualities were completely lacking on the Russian side. This doesn't mean, however, that a Bradley (or any other modern) Infantry Fighting Vehicle is superior to a T-90 (or any other modern) Main Battle Tank. In this particular case, a superb crew was able to play out all the strengths of its weapon system against a nominally stronger enemy. The Ukrainians were faster and smarter than their Russian adversary. They mastered their vehicle and the situation. The excellent Bushmaster M242 25mm autocannon of the Bradley engaging (and finally destroying) a Russian T-90 (Picture: Ministry of Defense, Ukraine) It shows us how important training is. It has nothing to do with the “infantry undisputedly won the infantry vs tankers debate”. There’s no such debate in the first place. The infantry and armor of one side always work together against the other side and vice versa. Modern warfare is combined warfare. Question: How are you affected by the war going on in Ukraine?
Answer: I haven’t slept much since the Russian invasion started, that much is sure. At my age, sleeping is maybe the greatest pleasure life has to offer. As I work in Ukraine to support soldiers in the Armed Forces, I also haven’t seen many of my pre-war friends for a long time. I think these are the only negative effects. At an army base near the frontline in Donetsk. On the upside, I made a lot of new friends. People from all over the planet: Ukrainians, Poles, Brits, Canadians, South Africans, and even an Argentinian. The best thing, however, is that I can do something I like and where I’m good at. Despite the long working hours, the stress, and the (occasional) dangerous moments, I wouldn't want to change places with anyone in the world.

Question: Can every military member be called into combat despite having a non-combat MOS?
Answer: Yes. It doesn’t matter if you work as a cook or a clerk, every soldier is a rifleman. I sometimes have to explain this to people in Ukraine: After you signed up for the military, you may indeed be working in this or that non-combat job, but there's no guarantee. There’s also no guarantee that you won't have to serve longer than the time specified in your contract. The moment you sign your contract, you more or less sign away all of your rights. A protest of family members of service personnel in Ukraine. They protest that the army most probably won't honor the 3-year duration term of the service contracts most soldiers have signed. (Picture by the author of this post) This may be less clear (but is equally true) for peacetime armies. Once a war breaks out, all the peacetime promises are off. If there’s a need, a military clerk working in a cozy Air Force base in the United States may very well find himself in a trench in some godforsaken place in the Middle East. Question: What do you think the internal reaction is in Russia to the news that Ryan Evans, a Reuters safety advisor, was killed in Ukraine?
Answer: I read some posts from pro-Russian bloggers claiming that the Sapphire Hotel in Kramatorsk, where Ryan was killed, was a rallying point for "hundreds of foreign mercenaries” but this is, of course, rubbish. I've been to Kramatorsk many times, and I know the part of the city where the hotel is located. Since it's not too far from the frontline, Kramatorsk is full of soldiers and is often a target of Russian missile strikes (the air raid alert in this city rarely goes off). I don't believe this hotel was a legitimate target (it was a civilian object), but this has never stopped the Russians from launching a missile. Ryan Evans, the Reuters security advisor who was killed yesterday. (Picture: Ryan Evans) Ryan Evans, the security advisor for the Reuters journalists and a former British soldier, should have known this. Additionally, the hotel is very close to the city center, which has been a preferred target of Russian missile strikes in the past. The “Ria Lounge” pizzeria, where 13 people were killed in 2023, many of them journalists, is just around the corner. I feel sorry for Mr. Evans and the people who were injured during this attack, but they were in a place you would be better off avoiding. The cheap guest houses on the outskirts of Kramatorsk may not have air conditioning or a swimming pool, but the chances of being surprised by a Russian missile in your sleep are much lower there.
